title: Some social platforms create collective product traps: people use them for access while wishing the social system did not exist
source_unit: World Happiness Report 2026, Chapter 6: Social media, wasting time, and product traps
geography: United States studies summarized in the chapter, including a nationally representative adult sample, a Facebook deactivation experiment, and U.S. college-student evidence on Instagram and TikTok

observations.period: 2018 pilot and subsequent U.S. nationally representative valuation studies

denominator.unit: participants in the full Facebook valuation survey; pilot sample separately reported as 439

facebook_wtp_median.unit: US dollars per month people would pay to use Facebook

facebook_wta_median.unit: US dollars per month people would demand to stop using Facebook

zero_wtp_pilot.unit: percent of pilot participants willing to pay zero for a month of Facebook use

mechanism.value: Use can persist despite low reflective valuation because the social cost of leaving is larger than the price people assign to the product itself

observations.method: Chapter synthesis of willingness-to-pay and willingness-to-accept studies, including a nationally representative U.S. sample and an earlier pilot.
observations.uncertainty: WTP and WTA are vulnerable to anchoring, free-good protest responses, endowment effects, hypothetical bias, and different interpretations of use versus non-use; they are not direct measures of total welfare.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults, Facebook users and non-users, with platform-specific estimates reported for a wider set of social-media services.
observations.counterinterpretation: A high amount demanded to stop using a platform may reflect valued social connection, political information, or fear of losing access rather than coercion or low wellbeing.

observations.period: Facebook deactivation experiment; one-month treatment period

denominator.unit: Facebook users recruited for the deactivation experiment

deactivation_outcome.value: Participants assigned to deactivate were happier, more satisfied with life, less anxious, and less depressed across measured outcomes

effect_scale.value: The chapter reports the improvement as small but significant and approximately 25–40% of the standard improvement from group or individual therapy

post_treatment_use.value: Deactivation reduced later app use and increased the likelihood of deleting the app, but willingness to accept payment for another month off remained substantial

mechanism.value: Short-run wellbeing improvement does not automatically overcome network dependence, habit, information value, or fear of missing out

observations.method: Randomized deactivation experiment summarized in the World Happiness Report chapter; treatment and control groups were followed over a four-week period with wellbeing and later-use measures.
observations.uncertainty: The underlying study concerns Facebook users and a defined treatment period; it does not establish long-run effects, effects for every platform, or the relative importance of social connection, information, habit, and design.
observations.subgroup: U.S. Facebook users recruited through Facebook advertising, with outcomes measured across subjective wellbeing dimensions.
observations.counterinterpretation: A month off may produce novelty or temporary relief while reducing access to relationships or political information; the chapter notes that the control group had more political knowledge on one measured dimension.

observations.period: U.S. college-student studies of community-level platform shutdown preferences

denominator.unit: community-level valuation design comparing individual deactivation with collective deactivation

tiktok_individual_wta.unit: US dollars per month college students would demand to deactivate TikTok individually

instagram_individual_wta.unit: US dollars per month college students would demand to deactivate Instagram individually

tiktok_collective_wtp.unit: US dollars students would pay for their whole community to deactivate TikTok for a month

instagram_collective_wtp.unit: US dollars students would pay for their whole community to deactivate Instagram for a month

mechanism.value: The same product can be individually useful yet collectively undesirable when opting out threatens social position, information access, or relationships

observations.method: Chapter synthesis of community-contingent willingness-to-pay and individual willingness-to-accept measures among U.S. college students.
observations.uncertainty: The population is a college-student sample and the valuations are hypothetical; the estimates do not establish platform-wide prevalence, causality, or the exact social mechanism behind the collective preference.
observations.subgroup: U.S. college students and active users of TikTok and Instagram; community boundaries are defined by the study design.
observations.counterinterpretation: Collective shutdown preferences may express dissatisfaction with current platform design while students still value the underlying social network, creator economy, or communication function.

observations.period: 2026 chapter synthesis; social meaning, opting out, and consumer agency

denominator.unit: conceptual synthesis of three empirical studies

negative_nonuser_externality.value: Non-users can bear costs from a platform’s existence because important interactions, signals, and opportunities migrate onto it

coordination_failure.value: Individual exit can be privately costly even when coordinated exit would make many people better off

wasting_time_good.value: Some users may continue a product they regard as low-value because habit, free access, social norms, or opportunity costs obscure the alternative use of time

consumer_agency_boundary.value: Observed use is not equivalent to endorsement, satisfaction, or unconstrained choice

observations.method: Analytical synthesis of experimental and valuation evidence in the chapter; mechanisms are presented as interpretations, not separately identified causal estimates.
observations.uncertainty: The product-trap framework is a useful mechanism for further testing but should not be generalized to all digital products, all users, or all forms of repeated consumption.
observations.subgroup: Users, non-users, communities, creators, advertisers, and people whose work, relationships, political information, or identity are mediated by platforms.
observations.counterinterpretation: Network goods can generate genuine value that individual wellbeing scales or hypothetical valuations fail to capture; social-media use can support knowledge, coordination, and belonging even when it also creates burdens.

related_sources.claim: Complementary World Happiness Report 2026 chapter on internet use, social connection, trust, peer saturation, and generational wellbeing.
Underlying randomized Facebook deactivation study cited by the chapter.
Underlying collective product-trap study cited by the chapter.

boundary: This record adds a consumer-culture and platform-dependence route from repeated use and network effects through time valuation, wellbeing, social pressure, information access, coordination failure, and collective agency. It synthesizes studies summarized in a World Happiness Report chapter; it is not a respondent-level reanalysis, not representative evidence for all platforms or populations, and not proof that any platform should be eliminated.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official World Happiness Report 2026 Chapter 6 PDF was reviewed for the valuation studies, Facebook deactivation experiment, community-level Instagram/TikTok preferences, negative non-user externality, and product-trap interpretation.
